trap_notes.d: The Tenth Amendment reserves powers to states, whereas Congress used federal commerce power.
trap_notes.default: The Court upheld the 1964 Civil Rights Act using Congress's Commerce Clause power.

prompt: How did Congress respond in 1973 to years of undeclared presidential war-making in Vietnam?

options.text: It passed the War Powers Resolution requiring presidential notice and time limits
It ratified a constitutional amendment abolishing the U.S. Air Force
It gave the Supreme Court sole authority to command combat troops abroad
It renewed the 1964 Gulf of Tonkin Resolution for twenty more years

explanation: Overriding Nixon's veto, Congress passed the 1973 War Powers Resolution to reassert legislative checks on troop deployments.

trap_notes.b: No amendment abolished the Air Force; Congress kept funding defense.
trap_notes.c: The president remains commander-in-chief, checked by Congress's war and funding powers.
trap_notes.d: Congress had already repealed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in 1971.
trap_notes.default: The 1973 War Powers Resolution aimed to check open-ended presidential deployments.

prompt: How did the 1973 OPEC oil embargo trigger 'stagflation' in the United States?

options.text: Surging fuel costs drove up prices across the economy while slowing growth and jobs
Cheap Middle Eastern oil forced Texas wells to close and cut consumer prices
Federal price controls ended all inflation by doubling U.S. coal exports
Electric cars replaced gasoline vehicles nationwide within two years

explanation: OPEC cut oil supplies over U.S. support for Israel, quadrupling oil prices and combining high inflation with stagnant growth.

trap_notes.b: The embargo caused oil prices to spike sharply, not fall.
trap_notes.c: Inflation remained stubbornly high throughout the 1970s.
trap_notes.d: Electric vehicles were rare in the 1970s; buyers shifted toward smaller fuel-efficient cars.
trap_notes.default: The 1973 oil shock raised energy prices while slowing U.S. economic growth.

prompt: What drove the late-20th-century population shift from the Rust Belt to the Sun Belt?

options.text: Air conditioning, lower taxes, and defense and service jobs drew people south and west
Federal laws closed Great Lakes ports to all domestic cargo shipping
Free desert farmland under the 1862 Homestead Act expired in Ohio
New gold rushes in Florida replaced manufacturing in Detroit and Cleveland

explanation: As heavy industry declined in the Rust Belt, affordable air conditioning and aerospace/service growth drew millions to the Sun Belt.

trap_notes.b: Great Lakes ports remained open, though steel and auto manufacturing shrank.
trap_notes.c: The Homestead Act ended in 1976 and did not drive modern Sun Belt cities.
trap_notes.d: Florida's growth came from tourism, retirees, aerospace, and services, not gold.
trap_notes.default: Climate technology and shifting jobs pulled population toward the Sun Belt.

prompt: How did U.S. defense spending and Soviet economic stagnation interact in the 1980s?

options.text: Reagan's military buildup strained a weak Soviet command economy, aiding Gorbachev's reforms
U.S. defense cuts forced NATO to buy fighter jets from Moscow
Soviet consumer factories outproduced Silicon Valley in personal computers
The Marshall Plan paid the Soviet Union to dissolve the Warsaw Pact

explanation: Trying to match U.S. defense technology while facing low productivity pushed Gorbachev toward glasnost, perestroika, and arms deals.

trap_notes.b: U.S. defense spending rose sharply in the early 1980s, and NATO did not buy Soviet jets.
trap_notes.c: Soviet central planning lagged far behind Western computing and consumer goods.
trap_notes.d: The Marshall Plan ended in the early 1950s and never included the USSR.
trap_notes.default: U.S. military competition added pressure on an already struggling Soviet economy.

prompt: What constitutional tension did the 2000 Bush v. Gore recount dispute highlight?

options.text: A candidate can win the national popular vote yet lose the state-by-state Electoral College
The House of Representatives picks the president whenever a third-party candidate runs
Federal courts count all paper ballots directly in every U.S. county
State governors cast electoral votes without holding a public election

explanation: Al Gore won the national popular vote, but Florida's narrow margin decided the Electoral College after Bush v. Gore halted recounts.

trap_notes.b: The House chooses the president only when no candidate wins an Electoral College majority.
trap_notes.c: Local and state officials conduct elections; the Supreme Court reviewed Florida's recount.
trap_notes.d: Every state selects presidential electors based on popular vote results.
trap_notes.default: The 2000 election showed how the Electoral College can diverge from the popular vote.

prompt: What long-term safety net did the Social Security Act of 1935 establish?

options.text: Payroll-funded pensions for seniors and unemployment insurance
Free four-year college tuition for all high school graduates
Universal health insurance covering every private hospital visit
Guaranteed federal factory jobs for every adult citizen

explanation: Passed in 1935, Social Security created old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, and aid for dependent children and disabled people.

trap_notes.b: College tuition aid for veterans came later under the 1944 GI Bill.
trap_notes.c: Medicare for seniors was not added until 1965 under LBJ's Great Society.
trap_notes.d: Temporary work relief came from the WPA, not the Social Security Act.
trap_notes.default: Social Security created payroll-taxed retirement pensions and jobless insurance.

prompt: How did the 1935 Wagner Act strengthen American labor unions?

options.text: It protected workers' rights to organize and bargain collectively
It outlawed all factory strikes in interstate industries
It allowed employers to fire union leaders without cause
It replaced private labor unions with federal military boards

explanation: The National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act) guaranteed collective bargaining and banned unfair employer anti-union practices.

trap_notes.b: The Wagner Act protected the right to strike and organize.
trap_notes.c: The law specifically outlawed firing workers for union activity.
trap_notes.d: It created the civilian National Labor Relations Board to oversee fair elections.
trap_notes.default: The 1935 Wagner Act guaranteed workers' right to organize and bargain.

prompt: Why did the U.S. launch the Bracero Program with Mexico in 1942?

options.text: To bring temporary Mexican workers to fill wartime farm and rail shortages
To relocate Midwest steel mills across the Mexican border
To end all agricultural imports from Latin America during WWII
To grant automatic U.S. citizenship to every foreign tourist

explanation: With millions of Americans in uniform, the Bracero Program contracted Mexican workers for U.S. farms and railroads from 1942 to 1964.

trap_notes.b: U.S. steel mills stayed in American industrial cities during World War II.
trap_notes.c: The U.S. sought closer wartime cooperation and trade with Latin America.
trap_notes.d: Braceros were temporary contract laborers, not automatic citizens.
trap_notes.default: The Bracero Program brought Mexican guest workers to ease WWII labor shortages.

prompt: What did President Harry Truman order in Executive Order 9981 in 1948?

options.text: The desegregation of the United States armed forces
The internment of Japanese Americans on the West Coast
The creation of the Peace Corps for overseas volunteers
The immediate integration of all southern public high schools

explanation: After pressure from A. Philip Randolph and Black veterans, Truman ordered equal treatment and desegregation in the U.S. military.

trap_notes.b: Japanese American internment was ordered by FDR's Executive Order 9066 in 1942.
trap_notes.c: The Peace Corps was created by President Kennedy in 1961.
trap_notes.d: Public school segregation was struck down by the Supreme Court in 1954.
trap_notes.default: Executive Order 9981 ended racial segregation in the U.S. armed forces.

prompt: What dual purpose did President Eisenhower cite for the 1956 Interstate Highway Act?

options.text: Speeding commercial travel and enabling military defense and evacuation
Replacing all U.S. freight railroads with toll-free bicycle paths
Ending suburban home building to preserve inner-city streetcars
Connecting Alaska directly to Hawaii across the Pacific Ocean

explanation: The National Interstate and Defense Highways Act funded 41,000 miles of highways for booming car travel and Cold War defense.

trap_notes.b: The act built multi-lane motor highways, not bicycle paths.
trap_notes.c: Interstate highways actually accelerated suburban growth and streetcar decline.
trap_notes.d: The system connected the contiguous 48 states.
trap_notes.default: The 1956 Highway Act served both booming auto commerce and Cold War defense.

prompt: How did the Soviet launch of Sputnik in 1957 affect U.S. domestic policy?

options.text: Congress created NASA and funded science and math education
The U.S. canceled all satellite research to cut federal spending
President Eisenhower signed a treaty banning orbital rockets
Universities closed engineering departments to focus on farming

explanation: Sputnik sparked the Space Race, leading Congress to establish NASA and pass the 1958 National Defense Education Act.

trap_notes.b: Sputnik triggered a massive increase in U.S. space and research funding.
trap_notes.c: The Space Race accelerated rocket development rather than banning it.
trap_notes.d: Federal funds poured into university science, math, and foreign languages.
trap_notes.default: Sputnik prompted the creation of NASA and major federal science education funding.

prompt: How did Rachel Carson's 1962 book Silent Spring influence U.S. environmental policy?

options.text: It exposed chemical pesticide harms and helped inspire the EPA and DDT ban
It urged farmers to spray more synthetic pesticides on national forests
It led Congress to repeal the 1916 National Park Service Act
It ended federal regulation of clean air and river water quality

explanation: Carson's warning about DDT and food chains mobilized the modern environmental movement, leading to the 1970 EPA and 1972 DDT ban.

trap_notes.b: Carson warned against reckless chemical pesticide spraying.
trap_notes.c: The National Park Service remained intact and environmental laws expanded.
trap_notes.d: Congress passed the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act in the years after Silent Spring.
trap_notes.default: Silent Spring sparked modern environmentalism and federal pollution safeguards.

prompt: What major change did the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 make?

options.text: It ended 1920s national-origin quotas and prioritized family ties and skills
It banned all immigration from Asia and Latin America for fifty years
It required newcomers to settle only in rural Great Plains counties
It gave British and German citizens exclusive entry into U.S. ports

explanation: By abolishing discriminatory 1920s quotas, the 1965 Hart-Celler Act opened U.S. immigration broadly to Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

trap_notes.b: The 1965 law actually ended old bans and led to rising Asian and Latin American immigration.
trap_notes.c: Immigrants were free to settle anywhere in the United States.
trap_notes.d: The 1924 quota system favored northern Europeans; 1965 ended that favoritism.
trap_notes.default: The 1965 act abolished national-origin quotas and transformed U.S. diversity.

prompt: Why was the January 1968 Tet Offensive a political turning point inside the United States?

options.text: Televised attacks shattered official claims that victory was near, eroding public support
The South Vietnamese army captured Hanoi and ended the war in three weeks
Congress voted to send one million more troops into Cambodia and China
President Johnson won re-election by a landslide after the offensive

explanation: Though U.S. forces repelled the attacks, seeing Viet Cong fighters storm the U.S. Embassy widened the credibility gap and antiwar dissent.

trap_notes.b: The war dragged on until 1975; Hanoi was never captured.
trap_notes.c: Public backlash led Johnson to halt bombing escalation and seek peace talks.
trap_notes.d: Johnson announced in March 1968 that he would not seek re-election.
trap_notes.default: The Tet Offensive exposed a credibility gap and turned U.S. opinion against the war.

prompt: What principle did the Supreme Court affirm in United States v. Nixon (1974)?

options.text: Executive privilege is not absolute and cannot block criminal subpoenas
Presidents are immune from all congressional impeachment inquiries
Cabinet secretaries may destroy White House records after an election
Only state courts can review tapes recorded inside the Oval Office

explanation: A unanimous Court ordered President Nixon to release the Watergate tapes, affirming that even the president is under the rule of law.

trap_notes.b: The Constitution explicitly empowers Congress to impeach and remove a president.
trap_notes.c: The Court ordered preservation and turnover of the White House recordings.
trap_notes.d: Watergate was a federal criminal and constitutional case.
trap_notes.default: United States v. Nixon limited executive privilege and upheld the rule of law.

prompt: What historic agreement did President Jimmy Carter broker at Camp David in 1978?

options.text: A peace framework between Egypt and Israel
The reunification of East and West Berlin
The North American Free Trade Agreement with Canada
An armistice ending the Korean War at the 38th parallel

explanation: Carter hosted Egyptian President Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Begin, leading to the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty.

trap_notes.b: Berlin and Germany were reunified in 1990 as the Cold War ended.
trap_notes.c: NAFTA was negotiated under George H.W. Bush and signed into law by Bill Clinton.
trap_notes.d: The Korean War armistice was signed in 1953.
trap_notes.default: The 1978 Camp David Accords forged peace between Egypt and Israel.

prompt: What core approach defined President Ronald Reagan's supply-side 'Reaganomics'?

options.text: Cutting income tax rates and business regulations to spur private investment
Raising top tax brackets to 90% to fund new federal job agencies
Nationalizing private oil and airline companies under federal control
Imposing strict wage and price freezes on all retail grocery stores

explanation: Reaganomics paired large tax cuts and deregulation with higher defense spending, aiming to stimulate private economic growth.

trap_notes.b: Reagan slashed top marginal income tax rates rather than raising them.
trap_notes.c: Reagan favored privatization and deregulation, not nationalization.
trap_notes.d: Wage and price controls were tried by Nixon in 1971, not Reagan.
trap_notes.default: Reaganomics relied on supply-side tax cuts and deregulation to spur growth.

prompt: What landmark protections did the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990 establish?

options.text: It banned disability discrimination and required accessible public spaces
It created Social Security retirement pensions for workers over 65
It barred private companies from hiring workers under age twenty-one
It shifted all hospital licensing from state boards to the Pentagon

explanation: Signed by President George H.W. Bush, the ADA required reasonable workplace accommodations and accessible transit and buildings.

trap_notes.b: Old-age pensions were created earlier by the 1935 Social Security Act.
trap_notes.c: The ADA expanded employment access rather than setting a minimum hiring age.
trap_notes.d: The ADA is a civil rights law, not a military hospital licensing measure.
trap_notes.default: The 1990 ADA outlawed disability discrimination and mandated accessibility.

prompt: Why did the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) spark debate in the U.S.?

options.text: Supporters praised lower trade barriers while critics feared factory job losses
Supporters wanted higher tariffs while critics demanded a single currency
Congress banned Mexican agricultural goods from entering Texas ports
Canada withdrew from NATO to protest U.S. tariffs on lumber

explanation: NAFTA eliminated most tariffs among the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, boosting trade while prompting concerns over manufacturing jobs.

trap_notes.b: NAFTA lowered tariffs and did not create a single North American currency.
trap_notes.c: NAFTA expanded agricultural and industrial trade across the U.S.-Mexico border.
trap_notes.d: Canada remained in NATO and joined NAFTA.
trap_notes.default: NAFTA weighed freer continental trade against fears of offshored factory jobs.

prompt: What ongoing constitutional debate did the 2001 USA PATRIOT Act intensify?

options.text: Balancing national security surveillance against Fourth Amendment privacy rights
Deciding whether states can print separate paper currencies during wartime
Allowing the Supreme Court to declare war without congressional funding
Repealing the 22nd Amendment's two-term limit for wartime presidents

explanation: Passed after September 11, the Patriot Act broadened federal surveillance powers, sparking debate over privacy and civil liberties.

trap_notes.b: The Patriot Act dealt with counterterrorism and surveillance, not state currencies.
trap_notes.c: Courts do not declare war; only Congress holds the constitutional power to declare war.
trap_notes.d: The 22nd Amendment two-term limit was not altered after 9/11.
trap_notes.default: The Patriot Act sharpened the balance between security powers and privacy rights.
